```{r, echo = FALSE, message = FALSE}
library(tmap)
tmap_options(scale = 0.75)
```

## Motifs and textures

The [fill patterns](https://r-tmap.github.io/tmap/articles/adv_patterns) of tmap, such as hatching, dots, and bricks, are **motifs**: regular arrangements of lines or symbols, drawn in the pattern color on top of the fill color. Each motif is clearly recognizable, which makes motifs well suited for categorical variables. However, they are not neutral to the fill color: the eye averages the lines with the color underneath, so a hatched area looks darker (or, with white lines, lighter) than it is.

Three pattern types are different: `"terrain"`, `"mottle"`, and `"sketch"`. They are **textures**: irregular, random surfaces without a recognizable motif. They are designed to leave the fill color readable, so that they can be used for a second, *ordered* variable on top of a color, in particular the **uncertainty** of the values shown by the color. For these textures, the map variable `pattern_density` is the strength of the texture, from 0 (no texture) to 1:

```{r, fig.height = 5.5}
tmap_show_values("pattern", values = c("terrain", "mottle", "sketch"), fill = "#4A90C2")
```

Each texture gives uncertainty a different meaning:

| Texture | Looks like | Suggests |
|---|---|---|
| `"terrain"` | random relief, lit from the northwest | the surface is rough: uncertain heights (e.g. in 3D maps) |
| `"mottle"` | a poorly painted surface: patches of slightly darker and brighter shades | the color is not exactly known |
| `"sketch"` | a sketchy pencil drawing: the color only in pencil strokes, with paper in between | the map is a draft: the color is a rough indication |

The highlights and shadows of `"terrain"` and `"mottle"` cancel out roughly, so the average color of an area hardly changes, also at full strength. `"sketch"` does change the average color, since paper is drawn in between the pencil strokes: the stronger the texture, the lighter the area looks. So `"sketch"` works best when lighter colors do not mean lower values, e.g. with a categorical or a diverging palette.

## Example: uncertain estimates

In the [fill patterns](https://r-tmap.github.io/tmap/articles/adv_patterns) article, unreliable estimates are hatched. Since hatching changes the perceived color, only two classes are used there: reliable and less reliable. With a texture, the uncertainty can be shown as a continuous variable instead.

In this example, the share of high incomes is shown for the districts of the province of Groningen. Suppose these shares are estimated from a sample survey of 5% of the inhabitants (the data are not, so the standard errors below are only an illustration). The standard error of an estimated share $p$ from a sample of $n$ persons is $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$, so the smaller the district, the larger the uncertainty:

```{r}
gron = NLD_dist[NLD_dist$province == "Groningen" & NLD_dist$population > 0, ]
p = gron$income_high / 100
gron$se = 100 * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / (0.05 * gron$population))
summary(gron$se)
```

The standard error is mapped to `pattern_density`. With `tm_scale_continuous()`, the values are scaled linearly from 0 to 1 (by `values.range`), where the `limits` set which standard error corresponds to no texture and which to full strength. The borders of the municipalities are drawn on top, so that the districts can be related to them:

```{r}
gron_muni = NLD_muni[NLD_muni$province == "Groningen", ]

districts = function(pattern) {
  tm_shape(gron) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "income_high",
                fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 40),
                                                values = "-hcl.purples3",
                                                value.na = "grey90", label.na = "Not available"),
                fill.legend = tm_legend("High income (%)"),
                pattern = pattern,
                pattern_density = "se",
                pattern_density.scale = tm_scale_continuous(limits = c(0, 8),
                                                            values.range = c(0, 1),
                                                            ticks = c(0, 4, 8),
                                                            outliers.trunc = c(TRUE, TRUE)),
                pattern_density.legend = tm_legend("Standard error (%-points)"),
                col = "grey35", lwd = 0.6) +
  tm_shape(gron_muni) +
    tm_borders(col = "grey10", lwd = 1.6)
}
```

```{r, fig.height = 5}
districts(tm_patterns("mottle", grain = 0.25))
```

The large districts look evenly painted, and the small ones blotchy. Their colors can still be compared, also between districts with a different uncertainty. The patches should be clearly smaller than the areas (here `grain = 0.25`): otherwise, a small area may be covered by one or two patches, which then look like a different color.

By default, the shades of `"mottle"` follow smooth noise: a patch only borders on patches of the next darker or brighter shade. This may look like a surface, such as a density or an elevation, rather than paint. With `random = 1`, each patch gets a random shade, so that any shades can be neighbors:

```{r, fig.height = 5}
districts(tm_patterns("mottle", grain = 0.25, random = 1))
```

## Example: preliminary election results

`"sketch"` suits maps of which the colors are not final yet. In this toy example, three parties, A, B, and C, take part in an election, and the map shows the party with the most votes per municipality, on election night. In some municipalities, not all votes have been counted yet. The share of the votes that is still to be counted is mapped to `pattern_density`: the more votes still to be counted, the sketchier the municipality:

```{r}
gld = NLD_muni[NLD_muni$province == "Gelderland", ]
set.seed(4)
n = nrow(gld)
gld$winner = factor(sample(c("Party A", "Party B", "Party C"), n, replace = TRUE,
                           prob = c(0.45, 0.35, 0.2)))
gld$to_count = ifelse(runif(n) < 0.6, 0, round(runif(n, 5, 90)))
```

```{r, fig.height = 5.5}
tm_shape(gld) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "winner",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = c("#D95F02", "#1B9E77", "#7570B3")),
              fill.legend = tm_legend("Largest party"),
              pattern = "sketch",
              pattern_density = "to_count",
              pattern_density.scale = tm_scale_continuous(limits = c(0, 100),
                                                          values.range = c(0, 1),
                                                          ticks = c(0, 25, 50, 75, 100)),
              pattern_density.legend = tm_legend("Votes still to be counted (%)"),
              col = "grey20", lwd = 0.8)
```

The municipalities where counting has finished are fully colored; the others are only sketched, more roughly the more votes are still to be counted. The paper of `"sketch"` is always white, since it is drawn on top of the fill color; it does not show the background of the map, such as a basemap.

## Parameters

The textures have a few parameters, set with `tm_patterns()`:

| Parameter | Textures | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `grain` | all | size of the relief, the patches, or the width of the pencil strokes | 1 |
| `seed` | all | random seed: another seed gives another, equally random texture | 1 |
| `levels` | `"mottle"` | number of shades | 5 |
| `contrast` | `"mottle"` | factor for the differences between the shades | 1 |
| `random` | `"mottle"` | randomness of the shades, from 0 (smooth noise) to 1 (random per patch) | 0 |
| `angle` | `"sketch"` | direction of the pencil strokes (degrees) | 45 |

The values can be specified with `tm_patterns()`, or as specification strings, in which the parameters that are left out take their defaults:

```{r, fig.height = 7.5}
tmap_show_values("pattern", values = c("terrain(grain=2)", "sketch(angle=0)", "sketch(grain=2)",
                                       "mottle(random=1)", "mottle(grain=0.5,random=1)",
                                       "mottle(levels=3,random=1)", "mottle(contrast=0.5,random=1)",
                                       "mottle(contrast=2,random=1)", "mottle(levels=9,random=1)"),
                 fill = "#4A90C2", ncol = 3)
```

The grain is relative to the pattern spacing at density 1 (a quarter of a text line, so 1/20 inch times the `scale` of `tm_layout()`). It is not affected by `pattern_density`, which only sets the strength.

The textures are drawn in white (highlights and paper) and in `pattern_col` (the shadows of `"terrain"` and the darker shades of `"mottle"`). On a dark fill color, a dark gray `pattern_col` is hardly visible; a black `pattern_col` gives deeper shadows. `pattern_size` is not used by the textures.

## 3D maps

The texture `"terrain"` is especially suited for 3D maps, made with `tm_polygons_3d()` of the extension package [**tmap.mapgl**](https://r-tmap.github.io/tmap.mapgl/), where the height of the extrusions is a data variable. Rough roofs show that the height is uncertain:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(tmap.mapgl)
tmap_mode("maplibre")

tm_shape(gron) +
  tm_polygons_3d(height = "income_high",
                 fill = "income_high",
                 fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(values = "-hcl.purples3"),
                 pattern = "terrain",
                 pattern_density = "se",
                 pattern_density.scale = tm_scale_continuous(limits = c(0, 10),
                                                             values.range = c(0, 1),
                                                             outliers.trunc = c(TRUE, TRUE)))
```

When only the colors are uncertain, but not the heights, `"mottle"` or `"sketch"` is the better choice.

## Notes

* The textures are raster images, which are generated at the resolution of the graphics device (the `dpi` of `tmap_save()`). In plot mode, they require a graphics device that supports clipping paths (R >= 4.1), such as `png(type = "cairo")`, `pdf()`, or `ragg::agg_png()`.
* The relief and the pencil strokes cannot be finer than the resolution allows, so a small `grain` only has an effect at a high resolution.
* In view mode, the textures are drawn as image tiles, which keep their size on the screen when zooming, like the other patterns.
* The textures repeat in tiles of 1 to 6 inches, depending on the texture and the grain. Larger tiles would make the repetition even less visible, but take longer to generate.
